title: The couple who didn't want to marry
hookLine: Pippali and Bhadda, both longing to leave the household life, are married anyway and live as friends (commentary on AN 1.14)

cards: A young man in a rich brahmin family is told it's time to marry. He doesn't want to; he wants to leave home for the holy life. His parents keep pressing, so, the commentary says, he tries a clever way out.
He has a statue of a woman made in gold, and announces he'll marry only someone who looks like that. Surely no such woman exists.
The family's messengers carry the statue from town to town, and in a town called Sagala, they find her. Her name is Bhadda. And she doesn't want to marry either.

teach.h: TWO LETTERS, SWAPPED ON THE ROAD.
teach.b: This is the story the commentaries tell of Pippali, who will become Mahakassapa, and Bhadda Kapilani. First, the letters. Each writes to the other: I hear we're to be married; find someone else; I mean to leave home.
The story says the letters were stopped on the road and swapped for warmer ones, so the families got their wedding. Second, the wedding night.
They talk, and find they want the same thing, so they agree to live as companions, not as husband and wife.
A garland of flowers lies on the bed between them, and the story says neither crossed it. Third, the long friendship.

They run a large estate together and stay friends. The tradition doesn't present this as sad or cold; it presents two people who understood each other and kept faith with what they'd agreed. Fourth, the turn.

One day, the story goes, Pippali watches birds eating the worms turned up by his plows, and Bhadda watches crows eating insects in the seeds laid out to dry. Each feels the weight of the harm their wealth depends on.
So they shave their heads, put on simple robes, take up clay bowls, and walk out of the house together, while the people of the estate weep at the door.
Where they went from there is a story for another day.

how: The story of Pippali and Bhadda is told in the Theravada commentaries as the early life of Mahakassapa and Bhadda Kapilani.

o: a gift of land given to the monks
a vow of lifelong marriage without children

games.q: Pippali and Bhadda: tap the pairs.
p: swapped on the road for warmer ones
lay on the bed between them

s: Pippali agreed to marry because he had fallen in love
he wanted to leave home; the golden statue was meant to make the marriage impossible.
Bhadda also wanted to leave the household life
her letter said the same as his: find someone else.
they left home separately, years apart
in the commentary they walk out of the house together.

games.q: you're Pippali on your wedding night. the woman you married wants to leave home as much as you do. what do you do?
o: live as an ordinary married couple.
agree to live as friends, with a garland between you.
games.why: they talk it over and live as companions, a garland of flowers between them, until they can leave together.

practice: Bring to mind a couple you know, your own if you have one, or your parents, friends or grandparents, and look past the roles, the bills and the schedule for the friendship underneath.
Find one moment when they were clearly on the same side, and hold it for a while. If it's your own partnership, think of one thing you could say that a friend would say, then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Nekkhamma, renunciation. What Pippali and Bhadda both longed for, even though they married, until they walked out of their house together. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali nekkhamma, renunciation: leaving the household life, what both of them longed for.

carryVoice: Your line: two who wanted to leave. They waited, side by side, until they could. See you tomorrow.
